paragraphs.source_en: This vast shelter in a high position above the wadi has a long wall suitable for painting, but the images are accumulated only in one spot (Fig. 5-13). There are anthropomorphic figures, two almost life-sized, and at least three of them are female, other figures are too faded to be recognisable (Fig. 5-14). All the figures are located at the exact point of the wall where the ancient waterfall would have flowed. Here the intention to paint the figures in relation to water is even more evident than in the previous site of In Temeilt because these figures literally follow the waterfall as they are accumulated vertically, whereas the wall next to the waterfall is completely empty. New figures were thus added above the existing ones and not next to them; they were deliberately painted in that spot of the shelter which became wet during the rain.

paragraphs.source_en: Can we hypothesize in this case that female figures were related to water, possibly symbolising fertility? This is known from San ethnography where girls are associated with water and with rain in particular, as a symbol of fertility and the regeneration of both females and rain (Lewis-Williams 1981).

paragraphs.source_en: Under the waterfall with the paintings there are two deep kettles and numerous small ones at the point where the water passed before exiting the shelter (Fig. 5-15). Here again, the waterfall, paintings and kettles seem to be interrelated. As this pattern is recurrent in many Round Head sites it should not be considered accidental and it should be a matter for further research.
